title: Cross-Mine Critical Spares Pool and Inventory Cleanup
one_liner: An AI cleaner for mine SAP materials masters that frees cash from duplicate spares, then turns the informal WhatsApp groups of competing mines' maintenance planners into a contractual, insured rotables pool for mill motors, liners and haul-truck parts.
customer: Supply chain, maintenance and finance heads at mid-size copper and lithium operations, starting in clusters where operators are neighbours: Arizona, Nevada and Utah, Antofagasta, the Arequipa-Moquegua corridor, the Zambian Copperbelt and the Pilbara. They pay a share of freed cash, not an IT budget.
problem: A copper mine holds $30-150M of spares. Materials masters are full of duplicates and near-duplicates (the same bearing under five descriptions), often 20-30% of items, so mines overbuy what is on another shelf. They still stock out on truly critical items (mill drive motors, girth gears, transformers, big castings) with 12-24 month lead times. Meanwhile maintenance planners across competing companies already borrow parts from each other over WhatsApp groups. It works only among friends and has no contracts, insurance, condition guarantees or return terms, so it never scales.
solution: Step one is the wedge. A CSV export of the SAP MM data goes into an LLM pipeline with OEM and aftermarket cross-references, multilingual description normalisation and criticality scoring. It outputs a list of duplicates, surplus and dead stock, plus the freed working capital in dollars. Step two lists surplus and 'insurance spares' on a members-only district board with a standard loan, lease and sale agreement, third-party condition inspection (vibration, NDT), logistics and insurance. It works like airline rotable pooling: three neighbouring mines share one spare mill motor instead of each stocking one.
why_now: Large motors, transformers and castings have longer lead times because of grid and data-centre demand. Steel and copper tariffs make replacement parts pricier. Lithium mines are cash-starved after the price bust, and copper mines face cost inflation and grade decline, so CFOs are hunting working capital. LLMs can now normalise messy multilingual part descriptions at almost no cost, which was not economic three years ago.
revenue_model: 15-25% of freed cash (sales and avoided purchases only, not write-offs), a pool membership subscription ($1-3k per month), and an 8-10% transaction fee on pooled loans and sales, plus inspection and certification fees.
non_obvious_insight: The spares problem is legal and trust-based, not a software problem. The informal swap network is the real supply chain. The biggest saving is not selling dead stock, it is not buying the 'insurance spare' a neighbour already owns. Pooling is an aviation idea that mining has never adopted because competitors will not share data without a neutral third party.
first_30_days: Through ex-colleagues, offer a free 2-week scan of SAP MM exports (CSV) at two or three mid-size mines. Deliver a dollar value of duplicates and surplus and a target list. Sign a success-fee agreement with the first one that shows a big number. In parallel, seed a private 'list before you buy' board among 20 maintenance planners in one district using Signal or WhatsApp, to formalise the network before any software is built.

title: AI Provenance Audits for Game IP Deals
one_liner: Due-diligence audits, plus a signed process-capture plugin, that tell publishers and acquirers what in a game is verifiably human-made and what IP they actually own.
customer: Small and mid publishers, game aggregators and acquirers, and lenders (idea 1's future competitors). Festival and award organizers pay for finalist verification. They pay $1.5-6k per audit. Studios and freelance artists pay $0-199 for the evidence pack.
problem: Steam's AI disclosure is self-attested. In January 2026 the form was narrowed to player-facing generative content. About one in five store listings now disclose AI use, and players punish undisclosed use, including refund fights over late disclosure. The US Copyright Office position is that purely AI-generated material isn't copyrightable, so a publisher buying a game with heavy AI art owns thinner IP than the price assumes. Awards bodies have reversed honors after discovering AI use.
solution: Two parts. First, a local plugin set (Aseprite, Krita, Blender, Photoshop, plus git and Perforce hooks, and C2PA where available) writes a tamper-evident, timestamped hash chain of authoring events, with no screen recording. Second, an audit desk takes a shipped build and repo and produces an asset-by-asset provenance map: evidenced human, AI-assisted, or unknown. It adds a Steam-disclosure recommendation and a copyrightability memo prepared with counsel.
why_now: Valve's January 2026 form rewrite left studios unsure what counts. AI use is now mainstream (roughly 20% of listings) and controversial. Awards and festivals are getting burned. Publishers are adding AI warranties to contracts and want a way to verify them.
revenue_model: Per-audit fees, bulk pricing for publishers with catalogs, a per-finalist fee for festivals and awards, and a paid studio subscription for evidence-pack export. Artists get the credential free, which builds the network.
non_obvious_insight: Classifiers run on shipped assets are unreliable, and false positives on human artists are reputational poison. The only defensible evidence is process metadata captured at creation, which is nearly impossible to reconstruct afterward. So the buyer is the balance-sheet buyer who cares about IP ownership, not the player. Freelancers who want a 'verified human' credential to win commissions pull the tool into studios from below.
first_30_days: Hand-sell audits: contact 30 small publishers and aggregators, and do 3 discounted audits by reading source-control history and interviewing the team. Ship a minimal Aseprite or Krita plus git capture plugin. Pitch two indie festivals or awards on verifying their finalists. Publish an anonymized 'what audits usually find' write-up.

title: Neutral Referee Network for Drone Delivery Noise
one_liner: A $40 Remote-ID-plus-microphone puck network that logs every delivery-drone overflight, becoming the neutral record in neighborhood noise fights.
customer: City planning and council staff in suburbs receiving Amazon Prime Air, Wing or Zipline service, HOAs, plaintiffs' law firms building nuisance or trespass cases, and drone operators that want third-party proof they follow agreed corridors.
problem: Residents count passes by ear (one Richardson, TX resident logged 52 passes on a 'slow day'). The city says it has no authority over routes, and the FAA leaves route management to operators. Operators self-report their own flights, so nobody has authoritative, ground-level, timestamped evidence for complaints, environmental reviews, negotiations or lawsuits.
solution: Small tamper-evident pucks (ESP32 receiving broadcast Remote ID, plus a calibrated MEMS microphone) mounted on homes and utility poles. They log drone ID, operator, altitude, dwell time and dB(A) at the ground. Monthly overflight reports, corridor heat maps and legal-grade evidence packs are produced per neighborhood. It works like airport noise monitoring for a world with no airport.
why_now: Amazon is expanding drone delivery toward roughly 500 US locations by end of 2026, and September 2026 coverage shows resident revolts in Richardson, TX and Michigan suburbs. The FAA's final Part 108 BVLOS rule has been at White House review since July 2026. Remote ID has been mandatory since 2024, so every compliant drone already broadcasts an identity that cheap receivers can log.
revenue_model: Cities: $15k to $40k a year for a 30-to-60-node network plus reports. HOAs: $2k to $5k a year. Evidence packs: $500 to $2,000 each to law firms. Operators: $20k to $60k a year for verified community-compliance dashboards (with published methodology so neutrality is preserved).
non_obvious_insight: Whoever holds the calibrated, tamper-evident log becomes the referee. Cities and residents lack legal control of the sky but hold leverage through evidence in FAA environmental reviews, permits and litigation, and operators will pay for a credible referee to head off regulation.
first_30_days: Build 20 pucks and give them to residents in Richardson and one Michigan suburb. Publish an open weekly dashboard and send it to the local newspaper and council staff. Convert the first paying HOA, city pilot or law firm evidence pack by day 30.

title: Legal Price Bargaining Co-ops for Salmon Fleets
one_liner: Back-office software and staff that let independent salmon boats negotiate price as one bloc under the 1934 Fishermen's Collective Marketing Act, as the Bering Sea crab fleet already does.
customer: Member-owned fishermen's associations, starting with one district of 150-400 permit holders that sells to only 1-3 buyers (a Kodiak, Chignik, Cook Inlet, Prince William Sound or Southeast group, not Bristol Bay first). The association pays us. Its dues are collected as a small settlement deduction, about 0.25-0.5% of landed value.
problem: A salmon fisherman is a price-taker. The processor posts a base price and a bonus schedule in June, the boat delivers before it knows the final price, and the retros show up months later. Bristol Bay's average ex-vessel price went from $1.03 in 2025 to $1.72 in 2026, and 2026's $260M fishery came off only 30.1M fish. Nobody on the fishing side of that swing had a seat at the table. Meanwhile most skippers believe acting together is illegal price fixing, so the bar talk about a tie-up dies every spring.
solution: A compliance-first toolkit for member-owned associations. It includes counsel-reviewed charter and bylaw templates under 15 U.S.C. 521-22 and CFEC permit verification at sign-up. Members can vote by SMS. A firewalled clean team collects member-submitted price, volume and quality data. From that it builds a formula price tied to public benchmarks (wholesale frozen sockeye quotes, roe prices, yen and euro, canned prices) plus a quality bonus schedule. We supply the negotiators, contract templates (multi-year formula price, settlement deadlines, audit rights) and dues collection through settlement deductions. The association is the bargaining party and we are the vendor, so we never bargain or set prices ourselves.
why_now: The 2025 crash and 2026 rebound showed the fleet how much money moves on one posted number. Processors now compete with loyalty and quality bonuses (for example $0.15 for RSW, $0.05 bleeding, $0.05 chilling). Bonuses are a formula, and formulas can be negotiated. Cheap e-sign, SMS voting and LLM contract review make an association nearly free to run. The crab fleet's Alaska Marketing Association proves the model works in Alaska.
revenue_model: $2-5K/month retainer per association, or 10-15% of dues. On a $260M fishery, 0.25% dues is about $650K/year, so a full-district association is a $65-100K/year account. Later add multi-association benchmarking subscriptions and negotiation-support fees tied to price gains.
non_obvious_insight: The FCMA has let fishermen, not processors, bargain collectively since 1934. The fear that bargaining equals price fixing comes from the DOJ case where processors were the defendants (Pan Alaska Fisheries). Associations fail on operations, not law: no clean data, no dues collection, no fast votes, no credible fallback. Outsiders assume the fleet lacks leverage, but what it lacks is a secretary's office with software.
first_30_days: Pay an antitrust and fisheries lawyer $10-15K for a 10-page FCMA playbook. Pick one small port with a near-monopsony buyer and hold 10 harbor and Facebook-group sessions. Get 30-50 permit holders to sign a non-binding letter of intent. Run a members-only survey of what each boat was actually paid, timed for settlement season (Oct-Dec). Publish a 'your fleet vs. the benchmark' report. Aim for one association signed at a $2K/month retainer by February, before prices post in late spring.

title: Alpha-Gal-Safe Pharmacy With Verified Ingredient Sourcing
one_liner: A cash-pay pharmacy and lookup service that tells tick-allergy (alpha-gal) patients which pill in their cabinet is safe, by NDC and lot, and compounds the ones that are not.
customer: Adults with alpha-gal syndrome, who pay cash for a membership and for compounded fills. CDC estimates up to 450,000 people were affected in 2010-2022, concentrated in the Southeast, Midwest and mid-Atlantic and spreading. A second wave of buyers is allergy clinics, health-system pharmacies and hospital perioperative teams, who would pay a license fee for the database.
problem: Drug makers are not required to disclose whether gelatin, glycerin, magnesium stearate or heparin came from a mammal. The label says 'gelatin' and nothing more. The free Alpha-gal Information (AGI) mammalian byproducts database works at ingredient level, not for the exact NDC and lot in the patient's hand. A pharmacist verifying one drug spends 30-90 minutes calling manufacturers. Then the wholesaler switches generic suppliers, the excipients change silently, and a patient who has been stable for a year ends up with anaphylaxis or a 2 a.m. ER visit. Patients and their Facebook groups crowd-source this by hand.
solution: 1) Build an NDC-level sourcing ledger. A pharmacist team sends templated requests to manufacturers for written excipient-source statements, and an LLM parses the replies and DailyMed SPL excipient lists. Each NDC gets a tier (plant or synthetic confirmed, mammal-derived, unknown) plus the date and lot range. 2) Sell a 'Safe Fill' membership that dispenses only verified NDCs, pins the manufacturer with a do-not-substitute request to the prescriber, and alerts the member when a source changes. 3) Compound unavailable items into HPMC vegetable capsules. This fits the 503A 'significant clinical difference' allowance because a documented allergy is a patient-specific reason, unlike copy compounding. 4) License the ledger to health systems and allergy groups.
why_now: Alpha-gal is now recognized as far more common than clinicians assumed, and the lone star tick's range keeps expanding. Regulators and payers have turned hostile to copy compounding after the 2025 GLP-1 shortage ended, so the legitimate lane is narrow, patient-specific allergy compounding, and this idea sits squarely in it. LLMs make parsing messy manufacturer letters and SPL data feasible for a two-person team, which was not true three years ago.
revenue_model: About $14 a month per patient membership (lookups, sourcing letters, source-change alerts, substitution management). Dispensing and compounding margin on cash-pay fills ($25-60 per compounded fill). B2B database license of $5k-25k a year per health system or allergy group. Optional paid sourcing-verification requests from hospitals for one-off drugs.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce asset is not a list of bad ingredients. It is provenance per NDC and lot, which changes silently when a wholesaler swaps a generic supplier, and only the dispensing pharmacist sees the swap happen. Whoever holds a dated, manufacturer-confirmed ledger owns the trust of a patient group that currently does all of this by hand and pays cash for certainty.
first_30_days: Pick the 50 most-prescribed oral drugs plus anticoagulant alternatives. Send NDC-specific inquiry letters to manufacturers and publish a free 'verified so far' list to build search traffic and credibility. Join the alpha-gal patient communities and offer 100 founding members $9 a month for life. A pharmacist owner with a compounding license fills the first cash orders locally. Get a review letter from two allergists. File nonresident pharmacy license applications in the top tick-prevalence states, such as TN, KY, MO, VA, NC and AR.

title: The Neutral Verdict on Dad's Driving
one_liner: An independent on-road evaluation of an aging parent's driving that gives adult children a credentialed Green, Yellow or Red verdict, plus a graduated plan so nobody has to be the villain about the keys.
customer: Adult children aged 45-65 of drivers 75+ pay $349-449 per evaluation and $12 a month for monitoring. Later buyers are auto insurers, Medicare Advantage plans and long-term-care insurers.
problem: Taking away the keys is one of the most dreaded family confrontations. The parent hears loss of independence and the child becomes the villain. Doctors rarely intervene, DMV medical review is slow, and driver-rehab specialists have months-long waitlists. Families wait for a crash. AAA and AARP offer generic tips, not an individual, defensible verdict.
solution: Frame it as a safety tune-up and send a certified evaluator, an OT with driver-rehab credentials or trained retired instructors under OT supervision. They ride in the parent's own car on a standardized 45-minute route with scoring for gap judgment, lane keeping, hesitation and scanning, plus a brief cognitive screen. The report gives a Green, Yellow or Red verdict. Yellow means no night, highway or rush hour with a recheck in six months, optionally verified by connected-car data or a cheap OBD dongle with the parent's consent. Red comes with a transition kit of robotaxi and rideshare credits, grocery and pharmacy delivery, and a senior-center pass, so retirement feels like an upgrade. The evaluator is advisory only and DMV referral is optional.
why_now: The oldest baby boomers turn 80 in 2026. Robotaxis now operate commercially in a growing list of US metros, so a real off-ramp finally exists. Connected-car APIs make objective driving data possible with consent. Scarce driver-rehab specialists can be leveraged with standardized scoring and remote review.
revenue_model: $349-449 per evaluation, a $12 monthly monitoring subscription for Yellow-zone drivers, and referral or ride-credit margin on the transition kit. B2B per-evaluation contracts with insurers and Medicare Advantage plans that want fewer elder-driver claims.
non_obvious_insight: The product is a third party who absorbs the blame. Families are buying relational insurance, not a road test. The recurring money is in the Yellow zone, where a graduated restriction plan needs ongoing verification, which turns a one-off confrontation into a subscription.
first_30_days: Partner with 2-3 driver-rehab OTs in one metro, plus elder-law attorneys and geriatric care managers for referrals. Build the scoring sheet from published road-test protocols. Get liability coverage and a consent script. Run 10 evaluations at a $249 intro price. Recruit through caregiver-support groups and Facebook groups for adult children of aging parents. Publish anonymized case studies.

title: Second-Life Studio: Shelved Human Drugs for Dogs
angle: Pairing 2: Biotech tools/synbio/lab automation/AI drug discovery x Pets & animal health/vet shortage/pet insurance
one_liner: Mine the wreckage of failed human biotechs for safe, clinical-stage molecules that make viable dog and cat drugs, and broker them to animal-health companies.
customer: Animal-health business-development teams (Zoetis, Elanco, Dechra, Boehringer AH, Merck AH, Ceva, Virbac) and venture-backed vet-drug startups pay for screening and deal flow. Sellers (liquidating biotechs, bankruptcy trustees, pharma pruning portfolios) pay success fees.
problem: Roughly 300 'zombie' biotechs exist, and 2026 has brought 15,000+ biopharma job cuts across 50+ companies. Their clinical-stage compounds, with human safety and PK data in hand, are being abandoned because human markets need $300M+ peak sales. Meanwhile animal health has few new molecules for canine lymphoma and osteosarcoma, feline CKD, IBD or chronic pain, and about 80% of dogs with lymphoma never get IV chemo.
solution: A scouting and licensing studio. It uses AI to mine ClinicalTrials.gov, SEC filings, layoff and bankruptcy trackers for discontinued assets that were not stopped for safety. It scores each for target conservation in dogs and cats, allometric dosing, market size and eligibility for FDA CVM expanded conditional approval. It packages dossiers with a vet development plan and KOL letters, then brokers options, licenses or asset purchases, keeping a finder's fee plus equity or royalty in each spun-out newco.
why_now: The supply of stranded assets is at a peak (layoff tracker, 300 zombies, wobbling software-only AI-drug shops like Schrodinger). Precedents are proven: verdinexor, a human-oncology-origin XPO1 inhibitor, became the first oral canine lymphoma drug, and anti-NGF antibodies moved from human programs into dogs and cats. Pet owners increasingly want oncology and chronic-pain options, while roll-ups (GoodVets, Mars) create channels that can absorb new products.
revenue_model: $15-25k 'Vet Opportunity Screen' reports per target class. $25-100k option fees. Finder's fees of 2-5% of deal value, plus 5-10% equity or royalty in spun-out veterinary newcos.
non_obvious_insight: The human 'failure' threshold is a commercial threshold, not a biology threshold. A $50M-peak product is a rounding error to human pharma but a real business in companion animals, where the target biology is often the same. Zombie boards will sell for pennies, so a tiny studio can option assets that incumbents ignore.
first_30_days: Build a database of about 500 clinical-stage assets terminated since 2019 for non-safety reasons, and shortlist 30 with plausible vet indications. Email 15 liquidating boards and 10 animal-health BD leads. Sell the first two $15-25k target-class screens as paid retainers. Aim for the first option agreement within 4-6 months.

title: Exchange for Unused Grid Interconnection Headroom
one_liner: A market where owners of unused interconnection capacity and stalled queue positions sell time-sliced access to batteries and data centers that cannot wait for the queue.
customer: Sellers: owners of operating solar and wind plants whose interconnection is sized for peaks they hit only some hours a year, holders of stalled or zombie queue positions, and retiring plants holding transferable capacity rights. Buyers: battery developers, data-center developers and large electrifying industrials that need MW-scale grid access in under 24 months.
problem: Queues hold thousands of GW while data centers and storage developers wait years. Existing owners have real headroom and completed studies but no idea what they are worth or how to transfer them under FERC rules, so deals happen only through informal broker phone calls.
solution: Standardized listings: point of interconnection, headroom by hour profile (from public settlement and EIA data), completed studies and network-upgrade dollars already paid, and rule pathway (surplus interconnection service, co-location, capacity-right transfers). The platform screens deals, supports escrowed contracts and builds price discovery in $/kW-year. Later it offers time-sliced flexible contracts, for example a battery using a solar plant's line at night.
why_now: AI-driven load growth is hitting interconnection scarcity in 2026. FERC has pushed surplus and flexible interconnection, ISOs allow some capacity-right transfers, and hourly injection data makes headroom measurable for the first time.
revenue_model: 2% to 4% success fee on contract value, seller SaaS for asset managers ($1k to $3k a month for headroom analytics), and buyer-side search retainers.
non_obvious_insight: The valuable asset is not the megawatt slot; it is the completed study and network upgrades already paid for by an earlier owner, which cut years off the timeline. Most owners do not know their headroom is worth anything.
first_30_days: Use EIA and ISO settlement data plus queue files to find 150 solar plants with low peak utilization. Cold-contact 40 asset managers, sign one exclusive listing, and take a term-sheet conversation to 15 storage and data-center developers. Target one small (about 20 MW) deal for the first success fee.

title: Parcel-Level Rebuttals to Wildfire Insurance Scores
one_liner: Evidence packs showing a coarse satellite-derived wildfire score is wrong about one specific lot, filed under new statutory appeal rights.
customer: Independent insurance agents and HOAs or fire-safe councils in Colorado and California whose clients face nonrenewal or surcharges. Insurers' appeal desks are a later buyer.
problem: Colorado HB25-1182 (in force since July 1, 2026) makes insurers disclose the parcel's score, credit documented mitigation and offer an appeal. California AB 75, operative July 1, 2026, gives notice and dispute rights over aerial-imagery nonrenewals. But 'owners still have to prove their case', and many wildfire models lean on roughly 30 m fuel layers and stale imagery that misclassify irrigated, gravel-scaped or recently cleared lots.
solution: For each parcel, pull the disclosed model inputs (fuel class, vegetation density, distance to wildland) and overlay multi-date 15-50 cm satellite imagery showing vegetation change, roof material and clearance, plus dated homeowner photos. Produce a regulator-format rebuttal pack with a ranked list of cheap fixes, and give agents a dashboard that scans their whole book for likely score errors. The real edge is a growing database of which input errors insurers concede.
why_now: Both disclosure-and-appeal regimes went live in July 2026 and insurers' appeal desks are unprepared. Commercial constellations, including 30 cm Pelican and Vantor archives, plus 15 cm HD, have made high-resolution archives cheap. Regulators in CT, NH and PA say imagery alone is insufficient, and NY has a pending bill.
revenue_model: $149-$299 per parcel via agents. $10-$25 per parcel per year for HOA book scans. About $60 per appeal from insurers for standardised evidence intake.
non_obvious_insight: Wildfire scores are averages of coarse layers, so the cheapest way to change a score is often to fix an input error rather than harden the house. The resolution gap between 30 m models and 30 cm imagery is systematic, so a win on one lot tends to generalise to its neighbours and compounds into a book-level lever for agents.
first_30_days: Pick the Colorado Front Range. Recruit 5 independent agencies with 200+ WUI clients each, plus 2 HOAs. Run the first 50 score disclosures at a $99 pilot price per file, and track appeal success rate as the marketing asset.

title: Point-in-Time Certification for Alternative Data Vendors
one_liner: A vendor-paid, buyer-trusted forensic test that a dataset's history is genuinely point-in-time, extended to certify that an LLM-driven signal isn't leaking hindsight, plus a cheap timestamp 'witness' service.
customer: Mid-sized alt-data vendors and AI-signal startups ($2M to $50M ARR) selling to funds, at $15K to $40K per certification, about $8K per year to recertify, and $500 per month for the witness service. Fund data-sourcing teams use the reports free, which is what makes the badge valuable.
problem: Quants ask every vendor one question: 'when did you start collecting live?' The honest answer is usually that the history was reconstructed, with today's entity maps and taxonomies, overwritten revisions, and publication timestamps standing in for availability timestamps. Funds burn three to six months of trials before discovering this. Vendors lose deals, and every fund duplicates the same diligence. LLM signals add parametric hindsight, where the model's weights already know the outcomes of the backtest period.
solution: A standardized battery run on vendor samples under NDA. It tests for discontinuities at the claimed live date (coverage, missingness, revision rates, distribution shifts, entity-map consistency, timestamp-lag distribution) and for survivorship and delisting gaps. For LLM signals it runs black-box hindsight probes and entity-masked or post-cutoff re-runs. The output is a PIT Grade, a one-page badge and a machine-readable report. The witness service takes a daily cryptographic hash or snapshot of the vendor's feed, so in a year the vendor has third-party-provable live history.
why_now: Thousands of data vendors now sell into funds, banks and AI-agent builders who lack quant-grade diligence. 2025 to 2026 research (Look-Ahead-Bench, HindsightBench, detecting lookahead in LLM forecasts) has made LLM look-ahead bias a mainstream worry. Regulators are scrutinizing hypothetical and backtested performance claims.
revenue_model: Issuer-pays certification fees, annual recertification, a per-month witness subscription, and a premium hindsight audit for AI-signal vendors and allocators diligencing AI-driven funds.
non_obvious_insight: The only real proof of point-in-time history is a third party's timestamps, because vendor engineers routinely overwrite and backfill. Each buyer rediscovers this privately, so the cost is duplicated across hundreds of funds. Shifting the cost to the vendor, who wants the shorter sales cycle, is the arbitrage. Credibility requires published methodology and public aggregate fail rates, or it becomes a pay-for-grade scheme like pre-2008 ratings.
first_30_days: Open-source the PIT test suite on GitHub and publish teardowns of three public datasets. Get two or three fund data-sourcing heads to say they would use the reports. Sell five vendors a $7.5K 'pre-audit' in exchange for being named references, and launch the witness hash service to any vendor who asks.

title: Booth-Day Cover: Weather-Out Insurance for Vendors
one_liner: A $5-$15 add-on at booth-application checkout that pays vendors their booth fee plus a loss tier when rain, wind, heat or smoky air wrecks an outdoor event day.
customer: Art-fair exhibitors, farmers' market growers, food-truck and craft-fair vendors, sold at checkout through event organizers and vendor-booking platforms.
problem: Vendors prepay $150-$900 in booth fees plus travel and perishable inventory. When an event is rained out, wind-cancelled, or smoke keeps customers home, organizers rarely refund, and event-cancellation insurance protects only the organizer. The vendor is the uninsured party, and smoke-driven closures are increasingly common.
solution: Per-booth-day parametric micro-policies triggered by hourly station and radar data (rain over a threshold during market hours, gusts above a limit, heat index/WBGT, AirNow/PurpleAir AQI at or above 151). Payout tiers of $75-$500 are set by booth fee. Cover is sold via API in the booking checkout. Organizers get a 'weather-safe vendors' badge, a revenue share and a dashboard. Claims are automatic and paid to the vendor's payout account.
why_now: Smoke seasons since 2023 made AQI-linked outdoor closures routine. Hyperlocal sensor networks and 1 km radar rainfall data are cheap. Embedded-insurance APIs make per-transaction cover easy to bolt onto checkouts. A likely very strong El Niño (CPC/IRI, September 2026) points to a wet winter in the southern tier, where winter markets and festival seasons run.
revenue_model: Premium of about $6-$12 per booth-day at a 20-30% loading over expected loss, with 15-20% shared with the organizer or platform. Later, multi-event season passes and organizer-side cancellation cover.
non_obvious_insight: In outdoor events the vendor is the uninsured party, and a booth-day is a near-perfect unit of insurance: known date, place, price and trigger. The checkout is the underwriting file and weather data is the claims adjuster, so there is almost no claims cost.
first_30_days: Pitch two or three regional market associations and one art-fair or festival platform. Underwrite through a parametric MGA. Ship a Stripe checkout link with a simple rain/AQI/wind trigger table. Pilot 100 vendors at about $6 each across fall festival season and publish the first payout story.

title: Unwind Desk for California's 3-Day Car Return
one_liner: A per-return concierge that unwinds a cancelled used-car deal (lender, add-on administrators, DMV, sales tax, commissions) inside California's new 48-hour refund deadline. It then turns the return data into a return-risk pool.
customer: California used-car dealers, especially independents and BHPH lots that sell 30 to 200 used cars a month and have no back-office bench. They pay $195 to $250 per return, or a standby retainer. Later, insurers and MGAs buy the underwriting data.
problem: From Oct 1, 2026, SB 766 gives buyers a 3-day right to cancel a used vehicle priced at $50,000 or less. Within 48 hours of cancellation the dealer must cancel the contract and refund the buyer, less only the deductions the law allows for mileage and damage. That is easy to write and very hard to do. The cost of an unwind is the cascade, not the car. The dealer has to reach the lender that has funded or is holding the contract, cancel each service contract and GAP with its administrator, and charge back the F&I commission. It also has to reverse the title, registration and sales tax, refund the down payment and any trade, and document the vehicle condition to justify any deduction. Independents have never done this at volume, and one botched unwind creates a refund violation and a private-plaintiff claim.
solution: Unwind-as-a-service. The dealer forwards the cancellation notice. The desk runs a checklist workflow that notifies the lender, submits cancellations to administrators with the correct pro-rata or full-refund basis, prepares the DMV and tax reversals, calculates the refund and permitted deductions, and produces a compliance file that meets the two-year retention rule. A delivery-day photo and video capture link is bundled, because permitted deductions depend on condition documentation. After 6 months of volume, the desk holds the only dataset on return rates, timing and loss per return in a mandatory-return regime. That data is enough to price a per-unit return-risk cover (roughly $60 to $120 per used unit) through a licensed MGA or insurer partner.
why_now: The law takes effect Oct 1, 2026, so the first returns arrive within days. No US state has had a mandatory 3-day return on used cars at this scale. The 2025 to 2026 run of subprime stress, roughly 30% of trade-ins underwater and repossessions at about 3M a year, means many buyers will discover mid-week that they can't afford the payment. That is the buyer most likely to use the cancellation right.
revenue_model: Flat fee per processed return ($195 to $250). Standby retainer of about $99 per month per store for priority handling. Phase 2: 10 to 20% of premium as an MGA on the return-risk pool. Phase 3: license the cancellation-cascade workflow to DMS and eContract vendors.
non_obvious_insight: Nobody knows the real return rate. Everyone models it on Carvana's 7-day return, but the buyers who return are not typical, because the F&I office sees payment shock and buyer's remorse first. A 48-hour refund deadline is shorter than the time a lender, administrator or DMV normally takes to process anything, so the dealer's exposure is process failure, not vehicle depreciation. Whoever owns the process owns the data, and the data is what makes the insurance product priceable.
first_30_days: Write the cascade checklist by state and by lender for the 20 most common California indirect lenders and 15 administrators. Approach the California Independent Automobile Dealers Association and 10 high-volume independents. Sell a $99 per month standby plan with a guaranteed 24-hour turnaround per return. Handle the first 20 returns manually with a shared spreadsheet and e-sign before writing any software. Log every step's time and dollar cost, since that log becomes the actuarial dataset.

title: Blind Validation Enclaves for Clinical AI
one_liner: Confidential-computing sandboxes where a hospital's private patient data and a vendor's private model meet, and only a signed performance report leaves.
customer: Health-system AI governance committees and health-AI vendors (imaging, ambient scribes, risk models), plus payers and insurers of AI performance guarantees.
problem: Hospitals cannot validate vendor claims on their own patients because PHI cannot leave and vendors will not ship weights. Published metrics rarely transfer to local populations. The Joint Commission and the Coalition for Health AI issued responsible-AI guidance in Sept 2025 and planned voluntary certification, so buyers now need evidence.
solution: A managed enclave (confidential VMs and GPUs) deployed in the hospital's own cloud tenant. The vendor's container runs against local retrospective data. Attestation proves that the evaluation code was unmodified and nothing was exfiltrated. The output is a signed report on subgroup performance, calibration and drift, repeated quarterly as post-deployment monitoring.
why_now: Confidential GPUs became generally available on major clouds in 2025, health systems adopted ambient scribes and imaging AI at scale, and Joint Commission and CHAI guidance created a demand for third-party assurance. The vendor-paid validation model is visibly conflicted.
revenue_model: $25-75k per validation (split between hospital and vendor), $10k per quarter monitoring, and payer or insurer programmes.
non_obvious_insight: Neither party trusts the other with its crown jewel, and the usual referee (the vendor) is conflicted. A machine that both sides can cryptographically verify replaces the trusted third party, so the product is the attestation as much as the test.
first_30_days: Partner with one academic medical centre's informatics team and two imaging or scribe vendors for a single use-case pilot. Use an existing confidential-computing offering rather than building infrastructure.

title: Battery-Aware 3PL for Military Drone Fleets
angle: Pairing 2: Logistics & physical automation x Government/defense/municipal
one_liner: A defense-cleared logistics provider built for lithium-powered drones: storage, battery conditioning, kitting, hazmat pack-out and repair depot for the Pentagon's tens of thousands of attritable UAS.
customer: Drone makers winning Drone Dominance and Gauntlet orders (many are 20-100 person startups) and the units and National Guard armories receiving drones. Pricing is per-drone kitting and per-pack conditioning fees plus storage and repair labor.
problem: The Drone Dominance Program targets more than 200,000 UAS by 2027, and about 60,000 will be ordered from Gauntlet 2 winners. Winners are startups that suddenly need to ship thousands of units per month. Lithium cells self-degrade, have Class 9 shipping rules and need storage-state management. Units have no facility to store, cycle and repair thousands of batteries, so drones sit in supply rooms until packs swell. Ammo-style logistics does not fit consumables that expire.
solution: A sprinklered, hazmat-capable facility near defense-drone clusters. Services include kitting (drone, packs, props, spares), pack-out to Class 9 rules, storage-state conditioning and cycling of packs, RMA and repair depot, serial and provenance tracking for NDAA-compliant chain of custody, and battery-safe return and disposal. Build toward CMMC-ready systems for controlled data.
why_now: Gauntlets 2, 2.5, 3 and 4 create recurring order waves every 6 months. New US drone tariffs took effect Sep 2026 and China's export controls on batteries and motors raise the value of domestic chain of custody. Amprius' $75M award shows domestic cells are ramping.
revenue_model: Per-kit handling ($15-40 per drone), storage per pallet-month, per-pack conditioning fees and repair-depot labor plus parts markup. Multi-year framework agreements with OEMs.
non_obvious_insight: A drone is only useful if its battery is at the right state of charge in the right hands within 30 days. The Pentagon is buying like it buys ammo, but there is no logistics operator designed for perishable lithium consumables. The bottleneck is the last 50 feet: the unit supply room.
first_30_days: Lease 10-15k sq ft of sprinklered flex space near a drone-OEM cluster. Get DOT hazmat training and a fire-protection review. Sign one Gauntlet 2 winner for a paid pilot of 1,000-2,000 kits with conditioning and RMA service.

title: Market Rulebook Red Team for New Venues
one_liner: Turn a trading venue's plain-English rulebook into an executable model, then use adversarial agents to find manipulation exploits and propose rule patches before real attackers do.
customer: Operators of new or small marketplaces: CFTC-registered event-contract and prediction-market venues, tokenized-asset and crypto exchanges, carbon-credit registries, energy and capacity market operators, GPU-compute spot exchanges, and ad-auction platforms.
problem: Modern electronic markets are built for speed and transparency, which has 'created new attack surfaces and systemic risks', and they 'can be manipulated in ways unanticipated by their designers'. Venues test their matching engine software, but nobody systematically tests the market rules themselves (settlement sources, auction tie-breaks, position limits, fee rebates) for exploits. Regulators expect venues to show their contracts and rules resist manipulation, but there is no standard way to prove it.
solution: An agent pipeline. Step 1: an LLM converts the rulebook or tariff PDF into a formal mechanism spec (order types, matching rules, settlement, fees). Step 2: an agent-based simulator with attacker agents searches for profitable manipulation strategies (wash trading, spoofing and layering, oracle or settlement-source attacks, self-dealing through fee rebates, cross-market squeezes). Step 3: it proposes rule patches and re-runs the attacks as regression tests. Deliver a fuzz report and a CI-style re-run whenever the rules change.
why_now: DARPA's Intrinsic Market Resilience (IMR) program, with a proposers day October 1, 2026, abstracts due October 22 and proposals due December 7, 2026, explicitly bets that LLM automation plus rigorous modeling can automatically model market designs, find weaknesses and recommend repairs. New event-contract, tokenized and compute markets are launching faster than their rulebooks can be reviewed. LLMs only recently became good enough at turning long legal text into formal specs.
revenue_model: $25k to $60k fixed-price rulebook audit. $3k to $8k per month for continuous re-testing when rules or fee schedules change. Possible subcontract or teaming revenue on DARPA IMR or follow-on federal work.
non_obvious_insight: A rulebook is code that nobody compiles. DARPA is paying to build the compiler-plus-fuzzer, and the same tool works on any venue, so the government-funded R&D is a free market validation of the product category. The IMR page states the problem ('manipulated in ways unanticipated by their designers'), names markets from 'equities and bonds to energy and cloud computing resources', and describes the LLM-plus-formal-modeling approach: https://www.darpa.mil/research/programs/intrinsic-market-resilience-imr. Caveat: the public page names no specific exploits and says nothing about commercial adoption, so the private-sector demand (for example the CFTC's requirement that contracts not be readily susceptible to manipulation) is my inference from background knowledge, not from the DARPA page.
first_30_days: Pick 3 public rulebooks or tariffs (a new prediction-market venue, a public energy market tariff, a carbon registry methodology). Run the pipeline and publish 3 short teardown posts showing a concrete exploit and a patch. Email the compliance and product heads of 30 newly launched venues with their own teardown. Sell 2 fixed-price audits at $25k. In parallel, submit an abstract by October 22 or offer teaming to IMR prime bidders.

title: Water Due Diligence for Small-Business Acquisitions
angle: Pairing 1: SMB back office x Water (lens: succession x water risk)
one_liner: A 5-day, fixed-price water-risk report for buyers, lenders and brokers of car washes, farms, RV parks, breweries and other water-dependent small businesses, plus a sell-side 'water-ready' file.
customer: Independent searchers and SBA buyers, business brokers and SBA lenders on $500k-$10M deals in water-dependent SMBs: car washes, farms, orchards and vineyards, RV parks and campgrounds, breweries and distilleries, nurseries, laundromats, ice and bottled-water plants, mobile-home parks.
problem: The Boomer sale wave meets drought. The value of these businesses rests on a tap, a well or a priority date that nobody puts in the sale memo. Phase I environmental assessments do not cover water rights, capacity, curtailment or PFAS and nitrate exposure. Buyers are first-timers with no diligence infrastructure. Search-fund capital targets $5-50M, and sub-$1M cash-flow businesses have no comparable formal capital.
solution: A 10-page report covering the legal water source and priority date, well permit and yield history, utility will-serve letter, capacity and moratoria, tap and system development fees, discharge and pretreatment permits, source-water quality against 2027 PFAS monitoring and nitrate, drought-surcharge exposure, a curtailment scenario under the Colorado River framework or state freezes, and an EBITDA-at-risk and price-adjustment table. A contract hydrogeologist reviews and LLMs assist with records pulls. Sell-side version: a $900 'water-ready' file that defends price.
why_now: From 2026-07-04 an SBA 7(a) loan can be combined with a 504 loan for up to $10M, so more real-estate-heavy deals will close. The Colorado River decision (Aug 2026) and Texas's Aug 3 grid freeze show that water and utility access can now stop a business. PFAS initial monitoring lands in 2027. 49.6% of the US is in drought. First-time buyers have no template for any of it.
revenue_model: $1,800-$3,500 per buy-side report. $900 per sell-side file. $299/mo broker pre-screen subscription. Bulk per-deal rate for SBA lenders. Referral fees from acquisition attorneys.
non_obvious_insight: Drought risk in a water-tied business is binary, not gradual. One curtailment or moratorium takes terminal value near zero, yet brokers, lenders and CPAs price it at zero. Whoever can put a number on the tap gets paid by buyers (walk away or reprice) and by sellers (defend the price). Once one bank asks for it, it becomes a checkbox for every SBA deal in the region.
first_30_days: Pick two states. Contract a hydrogeologist or water attorney for the review step. Go to 10 business brokers who specialize in car washes, farms and RV parks and offer 5 free reports on live listings. Ask two SBA lender loan officers to trial it. Convert 3 to paid at $2,500 by day 60.

title: Ceiling-Camera Auto-Logging for Strength Gyms
one_liner: Cameras that watch the lifting floor and automatically log every athlete's sets, reps, load and bar speed with no phone.
customer: Independent strength gyms, CrossFit boxes, powerlifting clubs and high school and college weight rooms paying $199-499 per month.
problem: Progress tracking is the strongest retention lever in lifting, but manual logging is tedious so most members skip it, and coaches at high athlete ratios cannot see everyone's sets or spot stalls.
solution: Two to four ceiling cameras plus an edge box; vision models recognize the exercise, plate colors (load), rep count and bar velocity; lifters are identified by wristband or QR rather than faces; a coach dashboard flags stalls, form drift and missed sessions and a member app fills logs automatically.
why_now: 2025-26 vision foundation models handle exercise and object recognition at the edge on cheap hardware, and tightening biometric privacy laws push products toward non-facial identification.
revenue_model: $199-499 per gym per month plus $1.5-3k install; school weight-room licenses; velocity-based-training analytics as an add-on.
non_obvious_insight: The buyer is the coach or owner, not the member: automatic logging gives coaches visibility that drives retention and coaching upsells, a Hudl for the weight room. Avoiding face recognition sidesteps biometric-law exposure.
first_30_days: Install DIY hardware (about $800) in two friendly gyms, label two weeks of squat, bench and deadlift footage with plate detection, offer a free three-month pilot, and measure log completion and member retention to justify $299 per month.

title: Percentage-Rent Rails for Small Retail Strips
one_liner: Sales-linked leases with rent automatically swept from the tenant's POS, so independent landlords can fill dark restaurant and shop spaces and tenants stop dying under fixed rent.
customer: Owner-operator landlords of neighborhood retail strips and mixed-use buildings with vacancy, and independent restaurants and retailers seeking space. Platform revenue comes from landlords and processed rent.
problem: Higher rates and a squeezed consumer are closing independents. Landlords face 6-12 months of vacancy and costly tenant improvements. Percentage-rent leases align risk, but small landlords do not trust tenants' sales reports, so the structure has been confined to big malls.
solution: A standard 'base plus percent' lease template (a lower base of about 50-60% of market plus 5-8% of gross sales above a breakpoint). Rent is computed and swept automatically from Toast, Square or Clover data with tenant consent, and the landlord sees a live dashboard. Add leasing and brokerage, and a lender-facing cash-flow report so landlords can refinance on more predictable income.
why_now: Refinancing at higher rates pushes landlords to prefer occupied space. Rates just rose again and the consumer is K-shaped. POS APIs and embedded payments now make sales reporting verifiable and rent collection automatic for small operators.
revenue_model: 1-2% of rent flow processed, a leasing commission on placements, and a lender-reporting subscription. Optional financing spread for landlords.
non_obvious_insight: Percentage rent died in small retail because of an information problem, not an economics problem, and POS data solves the information problem. Because landlord income scales with tenant sales, the system flips the landlord from adversary to partner and wins in booms as well as downturns.
first_30_days: Recruit three landlords with vacant restaurant or retail spaces in one metro. Have a lawyer draft the lease template. Build Toast and Square OAuth plus ACH sweeps with existing tools. Sign two tenants on sales-linked leases and use their first rent runs as proof.

title: Neighborhood Block Wildfire Cover via HOAs
one_liner: Softer reinsurance isn't reaching homeowners, so aggregate a mitigated neighborhood into one certified risk that capital will price like a portfolio instead of 300 anonymous parcels.
customer: HOA boards and Firewise-style communities of 200-2,000 homes in wildfire states (CA, CO, UT, NM, OR) where members are being nonrenewed or pushed to FAIR plans.
problem: Nonrenewals are at records and carriers price parcel by parcel, ignoring community-level mitigation like hydrants, vegetation control, ember vents and evacuation routes. Reinsurance is softening (Jefferies expects declines through 2027) but primary policyholders see none of it.
solution: Community risk certification, drone-verified and re-certified annually, plus block placement with an MGA or coverholder writing group-rated homeowner policies backed by reinsurance or ILS capital. The HOA collects dues, funds a shared deductible reserve and enforces mitigation standards.
why_now: California passed three claims and nonrenewal bills on 2026-09-03. Cat bond issuance is a record $18.9B year to date. Softening means capital is abundant and looking for well-defined books, and nonrenewals are a midterm political flashpoint.
revenue_model: MGA commission of about 12-15% of premium, $40-$100 per home for certification, and an HOA subscription for compliance tracking.
non_obvious_insight: In a soft market capital is abundant, and what's scarce is a verifiable, homogeneous risk pool. An HOA is a ready-made legal aggregator with dues collection and enforcement powers, which solves distribution and adverse selection together.
first_30_days: Approach 20 HOA management companies and Firewise sites in California foothills and Colorado's Front Range. Offer a free community risk-certification report. Sign one pilot LOI and line up an MGA willing to quote a block program.

title: Court-Ready Estate Accounting from Bank Statements
one_liner: Upload the statements and get the court's accounting format back, so small probate firms stop losing money on the ledger.
customer: Solo and small estate and trust law firms, CPAs acting as fiduciaries, professional fiduciaries, and small trust desks at community banks.
problem: Inventories, receipts-and-disbursements accountings and trust accountings to beneficiaries take 10-30+ hours per estate. Each state and county wants a different format. Small firms bill flat fees or lose money, and errors cause objections and surcharges.
solution: Upload bank and brokerage statements (PDF or CSV). The system categorizes transactions into principal and income, ties to date-of-death balances, flags unusual disbursements, and exports state-format accountings. Start with California plus one more high-volume state (New York or Pennsylvania). A reviewer trail records every override. Later add fiduciary 1041 data and distribution schedules.
why_now: LLM document extraction only recently became reliable on messy statements. Revocable-trust use has grown with online will and trust providers, so more successor trustees face accounting duties.
revenue_model: $149-$399 per accounting or $199-$499/month per firm, with enterprise pricing for banks.
non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck in probate isn't drafting, it's the ledger, and the ledger is what judges and beneficiaries inspect. Whoever owns the estate ledger owns the workflow and the data for tax, inventory and distributions.
first_30_days: Pick California. Recruit 10 small firms through bar section lists. Process 20 accountings manually for $199 each while capturing the county format rules. Publish a sample output for lead generation.
